title: Tagliatelle with Slow-Cooked Ragu
subtitle: braised beef and pork ragu on egg pasta
excerpt: This is the more traditional version of Bolognese -- braised chunks of beef and pork that fall apart after several hours in wine and tomato. The result is coarser and more robust than a mince-based ragu. It takes time, but very little of it is active work.
sourceNotes: A long-braised ragu of this type is found across northern Italy, from the Emilian hills to the Veneto. Braising whole pieces of meat and then pulling them apart gives a richer, more textured result than mince.

recipe.freezeNotes: The ragu freezes very well for up to 3 months.
recipe.batchNotes: This recipe suits a large braise. Double the meat and freeze in portions.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make the ragu 1 to 2 days ahead. Reheat gently and cook the pasta fresh.
recipe.temperatureNote: Fan 130C / Gas 2 -- low and slow in the oven

content.text: Sear the meat hard before braising. A deep brown crust on the outside builds the flavour base. After that, low heat and time do all the work.

Heat the oven to 150C. Pat the meat dry and season well. Heat the oil in a heavy ovenproof pot over high heat. Brown the beef in batches until deeply coloured on all sides. Remove and set aside. Repeat with the pork.
Reduce the heat to medium. Add the onion, carrot and celery to the pot. Cook in the residual fat for 8 minutes until softened. Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute more.
Pour in the wine. Scrape the bottom of the pot to lift all the browned bits. Let it reduce by half. Add the tomatoes, bay leaves and the browned meat back in. Season.
Cover tightly and place in the oven. Cook for 2.5 to 3 hours until the meat pulls apart easily with a fork.
Remove from the oven. Lift out the meat and shred it roughly with two forks. Stir it back into the sauce. Add the milk if using. Return to low heat for 10 minutes.
Cook the pasta in well-salted boiling water until al dente. Reserve a mug of pasta water. Drain and toss with the ragu. Loosen with pasta water as needed.
Serve with plenty of grated Parmesan.

items.symptom: Meat is still tough after 3 hours
items.cause: Oven temperature too low or a lean cut used
items.fix: Return to the oven for another 30 to 60 minutes. Tough meat becomes tender with more time, not more heat.

items.symptom: Sauce is greasy at the top
items.fix: Skim off the excess fat with a spoon before shredding and serving.

content.text: Long-braised ragu is Sunday cooking in northern Italy. It takes most of the afternoon but rewards the patience. The shredded meat makes a sauce that no mince can match. Pappardelle or tagliatelle are the traditional partners.
